segments.translit: nirbharaparamānandamudito hi śāntis tam evārthaṃ dyotayati —
segments.translation: Delighted with [supreme joy]{paramananda} in its fullness, [Śānti]{p-santi} brings out that very meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: [Śānti]{p-santi}, delighted with [supreme joy]{paramananda} in its fullness, brings out ‘that very meaning’ (cp.15.m1). He does not say which meaning he has in view.

flags.note: Munidatta's nirbharaparamānanda, 'supreme joy in its fullness', is shin tu mchog tu dga' ba, 'very supreme joy', in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), and tam evārtham, 'that very meaning', is de lta bu'i don, 'a meaning of that kind'; the Tibetan closes the sentence (gsal bar mdzad do) instead of leading into the song. The sense is unchanged (cp.15.m1).
tam evārtham, 'that very meaning', has no antecedent in this segment (cp.15.m1); it presumably points back to what Munidatta has been expounding, but I have not supplied one in the English.

segments.translit:
saa samveiṇa ityādi | samyak pavijalajasaṃyoge svasaṃvedanānubhavasvarūpeṇa siddhācāryyo hi śāntiḥ | alakṣyalakṣaṇādivicāraṃ vikalpaṃ na gacchatīti | ye ye 'py atītā yogīndrāḥ | etadviramānandāvadhūtimārgavareṇa gatāḥ te 'py anāvartte mahāsukhacakraśarasi[ja]vane lagnāḥ |
tathā ca rativajre —
eṣa mārgavaraḥ śreṣṭho mahāyānamahodayaḥ |
yena yūyaṃ gamiṣyanto bhaviṣyatha tathāgatāḥ ||
segments.translation:
“[Self-awareness]{svasamvedana}…” and so on. [Śānti]{p-santi}, a [siddha]{siddha} master whose [true nature]{svarupa} is the experience of [self-awareness]{svasamvedana} in the perfect union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, does not go into [conceptual thought]{vikalpa}, the [examination]{vicara} of the [mark of the unmarkable]{alaksya-laksana} and the rest. Whatever [lords of yogis]{yogindra} there have been in the past, who went by this excellent [path]{marga} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, they too are fixed, never to return, in the [lotus grove]{nalinivana} of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}.
And so it is said in the [Rativajra]{tx-rativajra}:
This excellent [path]{marga} is the best, the great rise of the [Mahāyāna]{mahayana};
going by it, you will become [tathāgatas]{tathagata}.
segments.note: Munidatta makes line 1a describe [Śānti]{p-santi}, a [siddha]{siddha} master whose nature is the experience of [self-awareness]{svasamvedana} in the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}: he does not go into conceptual examination of the [mark of the unmarkable]{alaksya-laksana}. For the [straight road]{ujubata} he puts the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}'s excellent path; those who took it rest, never returning, in the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra} (cp.15.m2).

citations.quoted: eṣa mārgavaraḥ śreṣṭho mahāyānamahodayaḥ | yena yūyaṃ gamiṣyanto bhaviṣyatha tathāgatāḥ ||
citations.work: Rativajra (so named by Munidatta; not otherwise identified)

flags.note: Munidatta's paraphrase of line 1a (cp.15.m2) makes Śānti the one who 'does not go' (na gacchati for the song's na jāi) and turns the song's 'examining' into conceptual thought that Śānti does not go into; the true nature (svarūpa) becomes Śānti's own. The draft of 1a has the mark of the unmarkable as subject. I translate his construal as it stands and do not harmonize it with the draft.

Shastri's daṇḍa after śāntiḥ splits one sentence: I construe siddhācāryyo hi śāntiḥ with na gacchati, as the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) does (slob dpon shAn+ti pas ... rnam par rtog par ma song ba'o). samyak goes with the union, as the Tibetan yang dag par rdo rje dang chu skyes mnyam du sbyor ba shows.

śarasi[ja]vane: Shastri restores ja, giving 'lotus grove'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rdzing bu'i tshal, 'grove of the pond', which suits the unrestored sarasi vane, 'in the grove at the lake'. I follow the restoration, as the glossary's nalinivana does.

anāvartte is locative: either an adjective of the grove ('the lotus grove from which there is no return') or an abstract ('in non-return'). The Tibetan has phyir mi ldog pa, 'irreversible'. The word stands where the song has anābāṭā (1b), but Munidatta (cp.15.m2) does not present it as a gloss, and I have not marked it as the glossary term anabata.

Smaller differences in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): it joins examination and conceptual thought with dang ('examination and conceptual thought') where the Sanskrit has them in apposition, and renders alakṣyalakṣaṇa as mtshan nyid med pa, 'without characteristics'; it has gyur pas, 'having become [the path]', for gatāḥ, 'went'; in the Rativajra verse it has dpal dang ldan, 'glorious', for śreṣṭhaḥ, 'best', as if reading śrīmān.
Munidatta's lemma reads saa samveiṇa where the song has saa sambeaṇa (cp.15.m2); a spelling variant only.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārthaṃ dṛḍhayati | kulem ityādi | kule pratyekaśarīre bho mūḍhā bālayogin etadviramānandopāyamārga[ṃ] vihāya nānyo mārgasambhāro 'bhimukho 'sti |
tathā ca rativajre —
nānyopāyena buddhatvaṃ śuddhaṃ cedaṃ jagattrayam iti |
atha vajramārgavāmadakṣiṇe bāla vaṛe khādivikalpaṃ mā kariṣyatha bho bālayogin | yathā nṛpaś cakravarttī kanakapathadhārayā krīḍodyānaṃ praviśati tadvat yogīndro 'pi līlayā 'vadhūtimārgeṇa mahāsukhacakrakamalodyānaṃ viśatīti |
tathā ca virupākṣapādāḥ —
vajrotthānaṃ sadā kuryyāc candrārkkagatibhañjanāt |
anyathā nāvadhūtyaṃśe viśati prāṇamārutaḥ ||
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes that same meaning firm. “From [shore]{kula-shore}…” and so on. At the shore: in each individual [body]{body}. O [fool]{mudha}, [novice yogin]{balayogin}, apart from this [path]{marga} that is the [means]{upaya} of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, there is no other provision for the path that leads toward the goal.
And so it is said in the [Rativajra]{tx-rativajra}:
Buddhahood is not by any other [means]{upaya}, and these three worlds are pure.
Then: to the [left and right]{vama-daksina} of the [vajra]{vajra} [path]{marga}, do not form [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} about a hair, vaṛe, kha and the like, O [novice yogin]{balayogin}. As a [universal monarch]{cakravartin} enters his pleasure garden keeping to the golden road, so the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} too playfully enters the [lotus]{lotus} garden of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra} by the [path]{marga} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}.
And so [Virūpa]{p-virupa} says:
One should always make the [vajra]{vajra} rise, by breaking the course of the [moon]{moon} and the [sun]{surya};
otherwise the vital [wind]{vayu} does not enter the portion of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads ‘at the shore’ as ‘in each individual [body]{body}’; the [fool]{mudha} is the [novice yogin]{balayogin}: only this path leads to the goal (the Tibetan drops the negative). Form no concepts left or right; as a monarch enters his garden by the golden road, the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} enters the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra} by the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} (cp.15.m3).

citations.work: Rativajra (so named by Munidatta; not otherwise identified)

citations.quoted: vajrotthānaṃ sadā kuryyāc candrārkkagatibhañjanāt | anyathā nāvadhūtyaṃśe viśati prāṇamārutaḥ ||
citations.work: a verse Munidatta attributes to Virupākṣapāda (Tibetan bi rU pa'i zhabs, Virūpa); the work is not named

flags.note: nānyo mārgasambhāro 'bhimukho 'sti, 'there is no other provision for the path that leads toward the goal': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no negative. It reads lam gzhan gyi sdom pas mngon par bde bar 'gyur ba yin no, 'through the restraint of another path one becomes manifestly blissful', as if saṃvara (sdom pa) stood for sambhāra and abhisukha for abhimukha; read as it stands, it says the opposite of the Sanskrit. I translate the Sanskrit, which the Rativajra verse that follows supports (cp.15.m3).

bāla vaṛe khādivikalpaṃ is obscure and probably corrupt. bāla repeats the song's bāla, 'hair' (2b); vaṛe and kha are unexplained. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has skra'i rtse mo tsam la sogs pa'i rnam par rtog pa, 'conceptual thought even of the measure of a hair's tip and the like', as if the Sanskrit had something like vālāgramātrādi. I keep vaṛe and kha as printed rather than guess.
mā kariṣyatha is plural, though the address bho bālayogin is singular; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) attaches 'O novice yogin' to the simile that follows.

mārgasambhāra, literally 'equipment (or provision) of the path', and abhimukha, 'facing, directed toward' (also 'at hand'), are rendered 'provision for the path that leads toward the goal'; 'goal' is implied, not stated.

For kule pratyekaśarīre, 'in each individual body', the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang gi lus, 'in one's own body', and its lemma is lus, 'body', following its own version of the refrain (lus kyi ngo bo mi shes pa). In the Rativajra verse it has dag pa 'di ni 'gro ba'i bdag, 'this purity is the lord (or self) of beings', for śuddhaṃ cedaṃ jagattrayam, 'and these three worlds are pure'.

Munidatta names the author virupākṣapādāḥ, that is Virūpākṣa (cp.15.m3); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bi rU pa'i zhabs, 'Virūpa'. I link the name to p-virupa, since the glossary lists this form there, but whether he is the poet of song 3 is not certain.

In Virūpa's verse the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has nyi zlar 'gro ba gzhom pa'i phyir, 'in order to destroy the going into sun and moon', for the ablative candrārkkagatibhañjanāt, 'by breaking the course of moon and sun', and kun spangs 'char where the Sanskrit has avadhūtyaṃśe, 'the portion of the avadhūtī'.

kanakapathadhārayā, 'keeping to the golden road' (Tibetan gser gyi lam bzung nas, 'taking hold of the golden road'): the glossary entry kandhara suggests the golden road answers the song's kaṇḍhārā (2b), but Munidatta (cp.15.m3) does not quote that word, so I leave the phrase unmarked.

segments.translit:
bālayoginam adhikṛtya dvitīyapadam āha —
māāmohetyādi | māyā prajñā ca bhanyate | tatrābhiṣvaṅgo mohaḥ | sa eva mahāsamudras tasyāntaṃ pra(prā)māṇaṃ na prāpyate bālayoginā | atha tasmin sadguruvāhyabhelakaṃ vihāya nānyaṃ naubhedakādyupāyaṃ vā vidyate bho bālayogin | kiṃ bhrāntyā sadgurunāthaṃ na pṛcchasi | tāntaṃ kva bhrāntiṃ vidhūya śrīmukhe caturthānandopāyaṃ gṛhītvā tasya māyāmohasamudrasyāntaṃ pramāṇasvarūpaṃ kuru |
tathā cānuttarasandhau —
sarvvāsāṃ khalu māyānāṃ strīmāyaiva viśiṣyate |
jñānatrayaprabhedo 'yaṃ sphuṭam atraiva lakṣyate ||
segments.translation:
With the [novice yogin]{balayogin} in view he speaks the second [verse]{pada}:
“Of the [ocean of illusion and delusion]{mayamoha-samudra}…” and so on. [Illusion]{maya} is also called [wisdom]{prajna}. Attachment to it is [delusion]{moha}. That itself is the great [ocean]{ocean}: its end, its measure, is not reached by the [novice yogin]{balayogin}. Then, on it, apart from the [raft]{bhela} steered by the true [guru]{guru}, there is no other [means]{upaya}, such as a [boat]{boat} of some kind, O [novice yogin]{balayogin}. Why, in [confusion]{bhranti}, do you not ask the true [guru]{guru}, the [lord]{natha}? Shake off that [confusion]{bhranti}, take from his glorious mouth the [means]{upaya} of the fourth [joy]{ananda}, and make the end of that [ocean of illusion and delusion]{mayamoha-samudra} something measured in its [true nature]{svarupa}.
And so it is said in the [Anuttarasandhi]{tx-anuttarasandhi}:
Of all [illusions]{maya}, indeed, the illusion of woman alone excels;
in it alone this distinction of the three knowledges is clearly seen.
segments.note: Munidatta says [māyā]{maya} is also called [wisdom]{prajna}, and attachment to it is [delusion]{moha}: that is the great ocean whose measure the [novice yogin]{balayogin} cannot reach. Only the [raft]{bhela} the true guru steers crosses it (the Tibetan: the true guru's word). The [lord]{natha} is the true guru; from his mouth the novice must take the means of the fourth joy (cp.15.m4).

citations.quoted: sarvvāsāṃ khalu māyānāṃ strīmāyaiva viśiṣyate | jñānatrayaprabhedo 'yaṃ sphuṭam atraiva lakṣyate ||
citations.work: Anuttarasandhi (so named by Munidatta; Tibetan bla na med pa'i mtshams sbyor)

flags.note: sadguruvāhyabhelaka, 'the raft steered (vāhya, literally 'to be conveyed') by the true guru': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has bla ma dam pa'i gsung gis, 'by the true guru's word', as if reading vākya for vāhya. The Tibetan thus makes the raft the guru's word; Munidatta's Sanskrit (cp.15.m4) makes it a raft the guru plies.

tāntaṃ kva bhrāntiṃ vidhūya: tāntaṃ kva makes no sense as printed; perhaps tāṃ tāṃ ca ('each such confusion') or tadantaṃ ca. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de'i 'khrul pa'i mtha' rnam par spangs nas, 'having cast off the extreme (or end) of that confusion'. I translate 'shake off that confusion'.

antaṃ pramāṇasvarūpaṃ kuru, literally 'make the end into that whose true nature is measure': presumably 'take the full measure of its end', answering 'its end, its measure, is not reached' just before. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has tshad ma'i ngo bo nyid du bya'o, where tshad ma usually means valid cognition (pramāṇa in the epistemological sense), though earlier it has mtha'i tshad, 'the measure of the end'. My 'something measured in its true nature' is tentative.

nānyaṃ naubhedakādyupāyaṃ vā vidyate has an accusative where vidyate wants a nominative; naubhedaka, perhaps 'a kind of boat', is uncertain. The Tibetan has gzhan gyi gru'i thabs kyang med, 'there is no other boat-means either'.

kiṃ bhrāntyā ... na pṛcchasi, 'why, in confusion, do you not ask': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) makes the confusion what is asked about ('khrul pa 'dri bar mi byed), as it does in its version of the song line (3b, 'khrul pa mgon la cis mi 'dri).

Smaller differences in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293): mi shes, 'does not know' (like the song's bujhasi), for na prāpyate, 'is not reached'; mtha'i tshad, 'the measure of the end', for the apposition antaṃ pramāṇaṃ; dpal gyi bla ma'i zhal las, 'from the mouth of the glorious guru', where the Sanskrit has only śrīmukhe, 'from the glorious mouth'; and an obscure sgyu ma'i des pa thams cad las for sarvvāsāṃ māyānāṃ, 'of all illusions', in the verse.
pra(prā)māṇaṃ: Shastri prints an alternative vowel; pramāṇa, 'measure', is meant either way.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena vartmamāhātmyaṃ kathayati —
śūnyetyādi | asmin mārgañ ca prāpya prabhāsvaraṃ śūnyam iti kṛtvā ucchedaprasaṅga[ṃ] kṛtvā bhrāntyā mā kariṣyasi bho mūḍhaḥ | atraiva prabhāsvarapariśodhitasvādhiṣṭhānacittaṃ bhāvayan punar aṣṭasiddhir bhavatīti niścayaḥ |
tathā cāgamaḥ —
dagdhvā māyāpuraṃ ramyaṃ sahasā jñānavahninā |
paśyanti satataṃ śūnyaṃ divyanetrā hi yoginaḥ ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he tells the greatness of the way:
“In the empty…” and so on. Having reached the [path]{marga} here, do not, in [confusion]{bhranti}, take [clear light]{prabhasvara} to be empty and so fall into [annihilation]{uccheda}, O [fool]{mudha}. Right here, as one meditates on the [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} [mind]{citta} purified by [clear light]{prabhasvara}, the eight [accomplishments]{siddhi} arise again: this is certain.
And so scripture says:
Having burned at once the lovely city of [illusion]{maya} with the fire of knowledge,
[yogis]{yogi} with the divine eye constantly see [emptiness]{sunyata}.
segments.note: Munidatta says this verse tells the greatness of the path. Having reached it, the [fool]{mudha} must not, in confusion, take [clear light]{prabhasvara} as empty and fall into [annihilation]{uccheda}; meditating right here on the [self-blessing]{svadhisthana} mind purified by clear light, one gains the eight accomplishments again. A scripture adds that yogis, having burned the city of illusion, constantly see emptiness (cp.15.m5).

citations.quoted: dagdhvā māyāpuraṃ ramyaṃ sahasā jñānavahninā | paśyanti satataṃ śūnyaṃ divyanetrā hi yoginaḥ ||

flags.note: prabhāsvaraṃ śūnyam iti kṛtvā ucchedaprasaṅga[ṃ] kṛtvā bhrāntyā mā kariṣyasi has two gerunds and a prohibition with no object. I take the whole as the warning: do not take clear light as empty and so fall into annihilation. It can also be read 'having taken clear light as empty, do not in confusion fall into annihilation', making only the fall the error. The Tibetan ('od gsal stong pa nyid du bya ste chad par thal ba'i 'khrul par mi bya'o) is open to both readings (cp.15.m5).

The nominative participle bhāvayan does not agree with aṣṭasiddhir bhavati; I render 'as one meditates'. punar, 'again' (Tibetan slar yang), might also mean 'further'. The Tibetan attaches 'O fool' to this sentence rather than the one before.

Munidatta writes aṣṭasiddhi, 'eight accomplishments', not the song's aṭamahāsiddhi, and the Tibetan comment likewise has dngos grub brgyad (cp.15.m5). I link 'accomplishments' to siddhi rather than using astamahasiddhi's 'eight great accomplishments'.

In the verse the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lhan skyes ye shes me, 'the fire of innate knowledge', as if reading sahajajñāna° for sahasā jñāna° ('at once ... with the fire of knowledge'); rab dga', 'very delightful', for ramyam; and a last line in which yogis who constantly see emptiness 'are the divine eye itself' (lha mig nyid).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena tad eva nirddeśayann āha —
vāmetyādi | śāntinā siddhācāryyeṇa vāmadakṣiṇābhāsadvayaparihārāt sphuṭam iti kṛtvā bhāvaviṣayopasaṃhāraṃ kṛtaṃ | asmin pariśuddhāvadhūtīviramānandamārgeṇa gacchan san ghaṭakuṭīgulmadālakādibhayaṃ na vidyate | tṛṇakaṇṭakakhallavikhallakādyupadravaṃ nāstīti | athāha stabdhonmīlitalocane yuganaddhaṃ paśyatīti |
tathā cāgamaḥ —
karoti taratām akṣṇoḥ śira[sa]ś cāvanamratāṃ |
staimityaṃ cittacaittā(tā)nāṃ śūnyatā śūnyatekṣiṇāṃ || 15 ||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada}, pointing out that same thing, he says:
“Leaving the two roads, left…” and so on. [Śānti]{p-santi}, the [siddha]{siddha} master, making it plain by avoiding the pair of [appearances]{abhasa}, [left and right]{vama-daksina}, has made the [summing up]{upasamhara} of the objects of existence. For one going by this [path]{marga} of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda} in the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}, there is no fear of [toll stations]{ghata}, [guard posts]{gulma}, dālakas and the like. There is no trouble from grass, thorns, pits, hollows and the like. Then he says: with [eyes]{eye} fixed and open, one sees [coupled union]{yuganaddha}.
And so scripture says:
[Emptiness]{sunyata} brings a trembling of the [eyes]{eye} and a bowing of the head,
and a stillness of [mind]{citta} and mental factors, to those who gaze at emptiness.
segments.note: Munidatta says [Śānti]{p-santi}, avoiding the pair of [appearances]{abhasa}, left and right, effects the upasaṃhāra (summing up, or withdrawal) of the objects of existence. On the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}'s path there is no fear of toll or guard post. One sees [coupled union]{yuganaddha} with eyes fixed and open; the song has them closed, the Tibetan comment half-closed (cp.15.m6).

citations.quoted: karoti taratām akṣṇoḥ śira[sa]ś cāvanamratāṃ | staimityaṃ cittacaittā(tā)nāṃ śūnyatā śūnyatekṣiṇāṃ ||

flags.note: stabdhonmīlitalocane, 'with eyes fixed and open', stands where the song has ākhi bujia, 'with eyes closed' (5b); I do not harmonize them. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mig zim bu mi g.yo ba'i mig zung, 'with the pair of eyes half-closed and unmoving', and has one 'see perfectly' (yang dag par mthong) without naming coupled union (cp.15.m6).

bhāvaviṣayopasaṃhāraṃ kṛtaṃ: upasaṃhāra is the usual word for a summing up or conclusion, and probably answers the song's saṃkeliu; it also means drawing in, withdrawal, which suits the avoidance of the two appearances. I use the glossary's 'summing up'; the glossary's own definition of upasamhara takes Munidatta's sense here as withdrawal (cp.15.m6). bhāvaviṣaya, 'objects of existence' (or 'existent objects'), is left unlinked rather than given visaya's 'sense objects'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads lho byang gi snang ba gnyis yongs su sdud pa gsal por byas nas yul gyi dngos por nye bar sdud par byed do, 'having plainly gathered in the two appearances of south and north, he draws them together into the entity of objects': it renders parihāra, 'avoiding', as a gathering in, and calls left and right south and north, as in its version of the song line (lho byang).

dālaka is unexplained; perhaps 'cleft, gully' (from dal-, 'split'), or a vernacular word such as ḍāl, 'branch'. The Tibetan list has 'phrang, 'narrow pass, defile', and adds 'gag, 'barrier', as its version of the song line does. I leave dālaka untranslated.

khallavikhallaka: khalla is 'pit, hollow'; vikhallaka looks like a jingling echo, so 'pits, hollows'. The Tibetan has rtsa dang tsher ma dngos, 'grass, thorns and dngos', where dngos may be a slip for dong, 'pit'.

taratām akṣṇoḥ: taratā is unclear (if for taralatā, 'trembling'; tara- can also mean 'quick'), and a trembling of the eyes sits oddly with Munidatta's 'eyes fixed and open' just before (cp.15.m6). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mig ni g.yo ba med byas, 'making the eyes unmoving', which would suit a reading such as sthiratā, 'steadiness'. I translate the printed word.

In the verse the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has sems nyid brlan pa'i sems, 'the mind moistened', as if taking staimitya as 'wetness' (stimita means both 'still' and 'wet'), and ends 'the eye sees emptiness as empty'. It introduces the segment as 'an extensive explanation (rgyas par bshad pa) of that very thing' for nirddeśayan, 'pointing out'.
gacchan san ... bhayaṃ na vidyate: the nominative participle is loosely construed with an impersonal verb; I render 'for one going'.

questions: cp.15.m2: the glossary lists Munidatta's (a)nāvartte as a form of anabata, whose English is 'anābāṭā'. Marking his Sanskrit that way would put the song's word into his mouth, so I translated 'never to return' and left it unmarked. Should anāvarta get its own entry (e.g. 'no return'), or be dropped from anabata's forms?

cp.15.m3: kanakapathadhārayā is likewise listed under kandhara (kaṇḍhārā). I translated 'keeping to the golden road', unmarked, and mention the possible echo only in a flag, since Munidatta never quotes kaṇḍhārā. Is that the right treatment?

cp.15.m6: for upasaṃhāra I used the glossary's 'summing up', but with 'the objects of existence' as its object and the avoidance of the two appearances before it, 'withdrawal' may be Munidatta's sense (the upasamhara definition already says so). Which should the English carry? Could 'withdrawal' be an alt?

cp.15.m2: Munidatta's paraphrase makes Śānti the subject of 'does not go' in line 1a, and the examining something Śānti does not go into; the current draft of 1a has the mark of the unmarkable as subject. Should the line's note record his construal as a divergence?

cp.15.m3: the Tibetan of 'there is no other provision for the path' has no negative and says one becomes blissful through another path's restraint. My note says only 'the Tibetan drops the negative'. Is that enough, or do you want a fuller witness note?

cp.15.m3: Munidatta's author is Virupākṣapāda; the Tibetan has bi rU pa'i zhabs. I linked p-virupa ('Virūpa') because the glossary lists the form there. Keep 'Virūpa', or print his form 'Virūpākṣapāda'?
cp.15.m5: Munidatta has aṣṭasiddhi, 'eight accomplishments', not the song's 'eight great accomplishments'; I linked 'accomplishments' to siddhi instead of astamahasiddhi. Acceptable?

Obscure words I kept or translated tentatively: bāla vaṛe khādi (cp.15.m3; Tibetan 'a hair's tip'), tāntaṃ kva (cp.15.m4), dālaka (cp.15.m6; Tibetan 'narrow pass'), taratā in the verse of cp.15.m6 (Tibetan 'unmoving eyes'). Do you want the Tibetan's sense in the English instead of the printed words?
cp.15.m2: I followed Shastri's restoration śarasi[ja]vane ('lotus grove'); the Tibetan rdzing bu'i tshal, 'grove of the pond', suits the unrestored text. Keep the restoration?
p-santi's English is 'Śāntipāda'; where Munidatta writes śānti (cp.15.m1, cp.15.m2, cp.15.m6) I used 'Śānti', as the draft does at 5a. Should 'Śānti' be added as an alt?
